text:
**For most people, LiFePO4 (LFP) is the better choice.** Nearly every current power station uses it, and the sources I found agree on why.

| | LiFePO4 | NMC |
|---|---|---|
| **Cycle life** | Typically 3,000-6,000 cycles to 70-80% capacity | Typically 500-1,000 cycles (one source says up to 2,000) |
| **Failure behavior** | Milder: lower peak temperatures, smoke rather than flames in lab tests | More violent: flames and much higher peak temperatures |
| **Weight** | Slightly heavier per Wh | Lighter at the cell level |
| **Price** | Median about $0.55/Wh in one database | Median about $0.95/Wh in the same database |
| **Cold charging** | Most stations won't charge below 32°F | Same limit in the manuals checked |

**Cycle life is the biggest difference.** A cycle is one full discharge and recharge. At one cycle a day, 500 cycles lasts about 1.4 years and 3,000 cycles about 8 years ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). For occasional use, such as a few outages a year, neither chemistry's cycle count is the limit. Calendar aging is ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). Check the percentage a cycle claim is rated to, because "to 70%" promises less than "to 80%" ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)).

**Safety is better with LFP, but it isn't fireproof.** In lab tests, LFP cells peaked far cooler than NMC cells. In one 18650 test the peaks were 259°C for LFP and 731°C for NMC ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). A 2020 overcharge study found the LFP cell actually hit thermal runaway earlier, though its failure was less violent ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). The U.S. Department of Energy also notes that LFP systems have had incidents ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). Use approved chargers and follow the manual either way.

**The weight advantage of NMC is smaller than it sounds.** The cell-level gap is large, but the case, inverter and fans weigh the same either way. In one database the median NMC station stored only about 10% more Wh per pound than the median LFP one ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). Some LFP stations are lighter per Wh than some NMC ones, so compare the actual specs.

**When NMC makes sense:**
- You need the lightest possible unit and will use it rarely.
- You already own a working NMC unit. There's no need to replace it.
- An NMC unit is steeply discounted and you'll use it only a few weekends a year. Be wary of an older NMC unit priced like an LFP one.

**An LFP example:** if you want home outage backup, the [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2) is a 2,073.6 Wh LiFePO4 station with a 2,600 W inverter and a 6,000+ cycle rating, and a 5-year warranty. It lists at $899, and the code AFF5OFF took it to $854.05 in a cart test on 2026-10-24. It is not expandable, and it weighs 24.2 kg (about 53 lb). That link is an affiliate link, so the site earns a commission if you buy through it, at no cost to you. Checkout has the final word on price.

Whichever chemistry you pick, check that the station's capacity and inverter output fit what you need to run, and read its charging temperature range in the manual.
